transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's... it's really about my job. I work as a cashier right now, which, you know, I have a bachelor's degree, so it's not exactly where I thought I'd be at 54, but it pays the bills. Or at least it does for now. I came in today because things have been getting really difficult at work, specifically at the register. I just keep getting stuck doing things that completely don’t fit the moment. 

It’s hard to explain, but it's like my body just gets caught in a loop or completely stops. For example, I'll be ringing someone's groceries up, and suddenly I just start tapping the scanner. Not just once, but in this specific pattern, over and over, tap-tap-tap, and I can't seem to just scan the next item. Or, and this is what really caused the big issue recently, I'll open the cash drawer to hand back someone's change, and my hand just completely freezes. I'll just be standing there, totally frozen with my hand hovering right over the bills, and the customer is just standing there staring at me, waiting for their money. I know they're waiting, I can see them looking at me, but I just... I'm stuck there. 

It’s incredibly embarrassing, honestly, and the customers get so impatient and agitated. The manager had to come over and apologize to the line, and it was this whole big scene. I actually got written up for it last week. My supervisor pulled me into the back office and said if I can't keep the line moving, they'll have to let me go, and I just... I need to figure out why I can't just hand people their change without freezing up like a statue.
Aside from these freezing and tapping episodes, have you noticed any shaking, stiffness, or slowness in your arms or legs at other times, even when you're not at work?

No, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm 54, so obviously I'm not as spry as I was when I was in my twenties, you know? Sometimes I get a little stiff if I sit in one position for too long, like when I'm watching TV on the couch in the evenings, but I think that's just normal aging. I don't have any shaking, like tremors or anything like that. My hands are perfectly steady when I'm eating or writing, or even when I'm just holding a cup of coffee. It's really just those specific moments at the register, like I was saying, where I get stuck tapping or freezing with my hand over the cash drawer. It's not a general slowness or stiffness throughout the day. It's very localized to those specific actions at work, which is why it's so frustrating and confusing. If it was an all-the-time thing, maybe I'd understand it better, but it's just so sudden and specific to those moments when I'm supposed to be doing my job.

Right before you start tapping or your hand freezes, do you notice any specific worry or fear going through your mind—like something bad will happen if you don't do it a certain way—or is it more like a physical urge or sensation that builds up and gets relieved once you do the movement?

No, it's... it's not really like that. It's not a worry, exactly. I mean, I'm worried about losing my job, obviously, like I said about the write-up and the manager pulling me aside, but right in that exact second before my hand freezes over the twenty-dollar bills or before I start the tap-tap-tapping on the scanner glass... there's no thought like, "Oh, if I don't tap this three times, the store is going to catch fire," or "If I don't hold perfectly still, someone's going to get hurt." It's nothing like that at all. I know some people have those kinds of thoughts, where they have to check the stove ten times or something bad will happen, but this isn't that. 

And it's not an urge, either. It's not like when you have an itch and you just have to scratch it, and then you feel better. There's no relief when I do it. If anything, it's the exact opposite of relief because the whole time it's happening, I'm just thinking, "Why am I doing this? Stop doing this, the line is getting longer, the customer is staring at me." It's incredibly distressing while it's happening. 

It's really more like... like my brain just sends a signal that gets stuck, or the signal just stops halfway down my arm. I'll be reaching into the drawer, fully intending to grab the change, fully knowing that the customer is waiting, and then... nothing. It just stops. The command from my brain just doesn't make it to my hand, or it gets scrambled into that tapping pattern. There's no fear right before, and there's definitely no relief after. It just happens, completely out of my control, and I just have to wait for it to pass while everyone watches me. It's just so bizarre, Dr. Smith, because I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing, I just... I just can't make my body do it in that moment.

Have you ever tried making that same motion—like reaching for change or tapping—at home or in a completely different setting, such as counting coins or tapping on a table, and if so, does the freezing or tapping happen then too?

Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith, that's what makes this whole situation so incredibly confusing and, frankly, so frustrating. I've thought about that a lot, actually. Because, you know, after that whole incident last week where I got written up—and I mean, I really can't emphasize enough how humiliating that was, having my manager pull me into the back office like I was a teenager caught stealing or something, all because I was just standing there like a statue with my hand hovering over the cash drawer while a customer stared at me—after that, I went home and I actually tried to test it out. 

I sat at my kitchen table, which is this old oak table I've had for years, and I got out a jar of spare change I keep on the counter. I just dumped it out and tried to mimic the exact same motion I do at work. Reaching out, picking up a quarter, a dime, sliding them over... and nothing. Not a single problem. My hand moved perfectly fine. I didn't freeze up, I didn't hesitate. I even tried the tapping thing. I took a can of soup from the pantry and ran it over the table like I was scanning it, and I just moved it across, one, two, three times. No urge to tap-tap-tap in that weird pattern, no getting stuck. I was completely in control. 

So it really does seem to be just at the register, in those specific moments when I'm supposed to be doing my job. Which just brings me right back to why I came in to see you in the first place, because I keep getting stuck doing things that completely don't fit the moment when I'm at work. It's like my brain knows I'm at the register, knows there's a customer waiting for their change or their groceries, and it just decides to either freeze my arm completely or make me tap the scanner in that pattern. And it's only there. It's not at home, it's not when I'm counting my own money, it's not when I'm doing anything else. It's just at work, and it's putting my job in serious jeopardy. I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I shouldn't be struggling to hand someone a five-dollar bill, you know? It's just so bizarre that it only happens in that one specific environment when the pressure is on, I guess, or when I'm in that specific role.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with sudden, situation-specific motor disruptions (hand freezing over cash drawer, stereotyped tapping on scanner) that occur exclusively in the work/register context and are absent when replicating identical motor tasks at home (counting coins, sliding a can across the table). There is no rest tremor, rigidity, or generalized slowness suggestive of a neurological/parkinsonian process, and the stiffness reported is attributed to normal positional stiffness, not a persistent motor sign. Critically, the patient denies any intrusive fear-based cognitions or urge-relief cycle preceding the behaviors (ruling out obsessive-compulsive or tic-related mechanisms), and instead describes the motor command as 'getting stuck' or 'scrambled'—a classic presentation of functional (dissociative) motor symptoms. The clear psychological stressor (fear of job loss, performance pressure, humiliation from being written up) temporally links to symptom context, and the inconsistency (normal voluntary movement replication in a non-stressful environment) is a hallmark positive sign for a dissociative motor disorder rather than a structural neurological, tic, or anxiety-driven disorder.
